title: Numbers in Words for Grade 2: Figures to Words the Easy Way + Free Quiz
meta_title: Numbers in Words Grade 2: Figures & Words + Quiz
meta_desc: Teach numbers in words for Grade 2 with a clear method for writing 3-digit numbers in words and figures, spelling traps fixed, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Your child can say ‘three hundred forty-seven’ but freezes when asked to write it. Here is the simple hundreds-tens-ones method for turning figures into words and back, with the spelling traps that trip up every Grade 2 kid.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 347 on a slate and most Grade 2 children will read it aloud without a hitch — ‘three hundred forty-seven.’ Now ask them to write those same words as a number, or to spell the number in words on paper, and you often get a long pause. Reading and writing numbers in words for Grade 2 is a genuinely different skill from saying them, and it is the one that shows up on every worksheet and exam. The good news: once a child sees a three-digit number as three neat parts — hundreds, tens, ones — the whole thing becomes a small, repeatable routine.

This is about number names only: turning figures into words and words back into figures, for numbers up to 999. I am not going to cover counting or place-value theory here — those are their own topics. What we are fixing is the exact gap where a child knows the number but stumbles on how to write it.

The three-part method for writing numbers in words

Every three-digit number splits into three chunks you say in order: the hundreds, then the tens-and-ones together. Take 347. Break it as 300, then 47. Say ‘three hundred’ for the 300, then ‘forty-seven’ for the 47. Written out: three hundred forty-seven. That is the whole trick, and it works for any number from 100 to 999.

The one habit worth drilling early: the tens and ones join with a hyphen. Forty-seven, sixty-two, ninety-one — all hyphenated. Children who learn the hyphen in Grade 2 stop losing marks for it in Grade 4. In my experience teaching seven-year-olds, the hyphen is the single most-corrected thing on their books, so it is worth making a small fuss about it from day one.

Going the other way: words to figures

To turn words back into a number, listen for the word ‘hundred’. Whatever comes before it is the hundreds digit; whatever comes after is the last two digits. ‘Five hundred sixteen’ → 5 in the hundreds place, then 16, giving 516. If there is no hundreds word at all, like ‘eighty-three,’ the number is simply 83.

The tricky teens and tens — where spellings go wrong

The method is easy. The spellings are where Grade 2 children actually lose marks, and it is almost always the same handful of words. The teens do not follow a tidy pattern, and four of the tens words drop or change letters you would expect to be there.

  • Four vs forty: four keeps its ‘u’, but forty drops it. Not ‘fourty’. This is the most common mistake I see.
  • Nine vs ninety: nine has an ‘e’, ninety keeps it — but nineteen also keeps it. It is the odd one that behaves.
  • Eight and eighty: both start with ‘eigh’. Eighteen and eighty share it too, so learn the ‘eigh’ chunk once.
  • Two, twelve, twenty: all begin with a silent-ish ‘tw’. Children who spell ‘twenty’ as ‘twoenty’ just need the ‘tw’ pattern pointed out.
  • Fifteen and fifty: five becomes ‘fif’, not ‘five’. So it is fifteen and fifty, never ‘fiveteen’.

A figures-to-words reference chart

Pin this near the study table for the first fortnight. It covers the exact words a Grade 2 child needs to build any number up to 999, and the trap-words are all in it.

The zero problem

Numbers with a zero in the middle catch children out. In 105 there are no tens, so you just say ‘one hundred five’ — you do not say ‘one hundred zero five’. Same with 400: ‘four hundred’, full stop. Teach children to simply skip an empty place rather than announce the zero. That one rule clears up most of the confusion around round numbers.

Practising without a worksheet

Number names stick fastest when they turn up in real life, not just on paper. A few things that work at home, all in Hindi or English — the skill transfers either way:

  • Read out the number on a bus, an auto, or a cricketer’s jersey and ask your child to write it in words.
  • Call out a price like ₹235 and have them say it, then write it, as ‘two hundred thirty-five’.
  • Swap roles: you write words, they write the figure. Getting it wrong on purpose and being caught is a favourite with this age group.

One honest caveat: do not rush to 999 on day one. Spend the first week firmly on numbers up to 99 — the tens and teens — because the hundreds part is the easy bit once the tens are solid. A child who has the tens spellings down cold can extend to hundreds in an afternoon.

Try the quiz, then the printable practice

Below is a free 8-question quiz on exactly this — matching figures to words, spotting the right spelling, and turning words back into numbers up to 999. Let your child work through it and read the explanations for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable Grade 2 worksheet at the end has graded number-name questions with a full answer key you can print as often as you like.

quiz.title: Grade 2 Numbers in Words Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on writing numbers up to 999 in words and figures, plus the spelling traps. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: How do you write 46 in words?
questions.explanation: It is forty-six. Forty drops the u from four, and the tens and ones join with a hyphen.
Three hundred is 300, and twelve is 12, so together they make 312.
Ninety keeps the e from nine. It is not spelled ninty.

questions.q: How do you write 105 in words?
questions.explanation: There are no tens, so you skip the empty place and say one hundred five, not one hundred zero five.
Six hundred is 600 and eighty is 80, so the number is 680. There are no ones, so nothing follows.
Five becomes fif, giving fifteen. It is never spelled fiveteen.

questions.q: How do you write 519 in words?
questions.explanation: Five hundred is 500 and nineteen is 19, so it is five hundred nineteen. Nineteen keeps its e.
Nine hundred is 900, ninety is 90, and nine is 9, which add to 999, the biggest three-digit number.

faq.q: Do I write 'and' as in 'three hundred and forty-seven'?
faq.a: In most Indian school books the answer is written without ‘and’ — three hundred forty-seven. Saying ‘and’ aloud is fine, but check your child’s NCERT-aligned workbook, as some accept both. Be consistent with whatever the school marks.

faq.q: Why does my child keep spelling forty as 'fourty'?
faq.a: Because four keeps its u and they assume forty does too. It does not. A quick way to fix it: write four and forty side by side and highlight the missing u. After a week of spotting it, the mistake usually stops.

faq.q: How do I explain a number with a zero in the middle, like 305?
faq.a: Tell your child there are no tens, so they simply skip that place: three hundred five. They should never say ‘three hundred zero five’. Skipping empty places is the single rule that clears up round numbers.
Not for number names at this stage. Grade 2 focuses on numbers up to 999 in most syllabi. Getting the hundreds, tens and ones pattern solid now makes larger numbers in Grade 3 far easier.
